Chapter 0 · Begin here

First, see the whole machine.

A quadcopter is a flying system that turns battery energy into four controlled columns of moving air. The pilot asks it to move; sensors measure what it actually does; the flight controller continually corrects the difference.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to trace three separate journeys: battery power, pilot commands and live video.

Make or buy in year one?

Make/own: original frame requirements and CAD, printed mounts, harnesses, assembly, firmware setup, inspection, test and records. Buy: motors, electronics, radio parts, camera, battery and propellers. We can own the product knowledge without pretending we can manufacture semiconductors or battery cells.

What you should understand now

Open each answer only after saying it aloud.

What makes the drone rise?
The motors spin propellers, accelerating air downward. The equal and opposite reaction pushes the aircraft upward. When total upward thrust exceeds weight, it rises.
Are the control link and video link the same?
No. Pilot commands travel radio → receiver → flight controller. Video travels camera → video transmitter → matching receiver/display. One can fail while the other still works.
What are we most likely to manufacture ourselves first?
The frame design and controlled production knowledge, printed mounts/fixtures, wiring harnesses, assembly, configuration, inspection, testing, traceability and packaging.

Chapter 1 · Flight

Four forces. Three rotations.

A quadcopter has no wings or steering surfaces. It moves by changing the speed of four propellers—hundreds of times per second.

↑
Thrust

Propellers push air down; the air pushes the drone up.

↓
Weight

Gravity pulls every part toward Earth.

↝
Drag

Air resists movement and spinning propellers.

⟳
Torque

Turning a propeller tries to twist the frame the other way.

Hover happens when the four propellers together push upward with the same force that gravity pulls downward. The machine is still working hard: if power stops, it falls.

How the pilot moves the aircraft

↥
Throttle

All four motors speed up or slow down together: climb or descend.

↶
Roll

One side pushes harder: the aircraft tilts left or right.

⌁
Pitch

Rear or front pushes harder: the nose tilts down or up.

⟳
Yaw

The pairs spinning one way produce more or less counter-torque: the nose turns.

Why four motors—and opposite rotation?

Four is the minimum common stable multirotor layout

Four independently controlled thrust points provide lift plus control around roll, pitch and yaw without complex mechanical linkages. More motors can add lift or redundancy, but add cost, mass and failure points.

Two clockwise, two counter-clockwise

Each spinning propeller twists the frame in the opposite direction. With equal clockwise and counter-clockwise pairs, those twists mostly cancel in hover. To yaw, the controller increases one pair and reduces the other while keeping total lift near the desired level.

Top view · normal quad-X idea
Front left ↺counter-clockwise
Front right ↻clockwise
Rear right ↺counter-clockwise
Rear left ↻clockwise

Centre of gravity: the balance point

The centre of gravity is where the complete aircraft balances, including its battery and payload. If the battery is far from the centre, some motors must work harder during level flight. That reduces control margin and can increase heat. A movable battery is therefore also a tuning and packaging decision.

Go deeper · the controller's loop

The gyroscope measures rotation. The pilot requests a rotation rate or attitude. The flight controller compares request with measurement, calculates an error and changes individual motor commands to reduce it. The loop repeats rapidly. Airframe stiffness, vibration and controller tuning affect what the sensors see and how safely corrections work.

What you should understand now

Why does the drone need four motors?
Four controlled thrust points let it create lift and control roll, pitch and yaw with a mechanically simple layout.
Why do neighbouring propellers rotate in opposite directions?
To cancel most reaction torque in hover. Changing the balance between the two rotation pairs turns the aircraft in yaw.
What happens if the battery moves away from the centre?
The drone becomes unbalanced and some motors must work harder merely to stay level.

Chapter 2 · Structure

The frame is the skeleton and the interface map.

It carries motor forces, protects electronics, positions antennas and camera, retains the battery, and keeps every propeller clear of everything else.

“Four-inch” and “500” measure different things

First-person view (FPV) means the pilot sees live video from the aircraft.

Current Prototype 1 direction

4-inch FPV

4″ prop

Compact, low-cost and cramped. “Four inch” normally describes propeller diameter, not wheelbase.

Candidate not built

5-inch FPV

5″ prop

More packaging room and higher energy. It needs more test space and a controlled bill of materials.

Reference platform

X500-style

≈500 mm

The number describes diagonal motor-to-motor wheelbase. Usually larger props, tube arms and payload decks.

Geometry changes the job

True-X

The motors form a symmetric X. Roll and pitch leverage are similar. Repeated arms are easier to manufacture and stock. Front propellers may appear in a wide camera view.

Dead-cat

Front arms are moved outward or back to clear the camera view. This helps imaging, but geometry is less symmetric and the controller configuration must match the real motor positions.

Propeller clearance is a hard interface.The rotating discs must never intersect each other, the frame, battery, straps, wires or camera—even after blade flex, assembly variation and minor crash deformation. Check with the exact propeller, not a drawing label alone.

Stiff enough, repairable enough

A frame that bends too much changes motor alignment and feeds vibration into sensors. A frame that is very heavy wastes energy. Replaceable arms localise common crash damage. Sacrificial flexible mounts can protect an expensive camera or antenna by failing first.

Make or buy?

Year one: own the frame requirements, geometry, CAD, drawings, revisions, printed mounts and inspection. Outsource carbon cutting. Later: bring cutting in-house only if safety, volume, lead time and full cost justify it. Purchased fasteners and raw laminate still require supplier control.

Dated retail snapshotCandidate frame: USD 22.95 · observed 4 August 2026; not a supplier quotation or volume-availability claim.

Why 250 g matters—but is not a claim

The Georgian Civil Aviation Agency portal describes a C0 class below 250 g and an Open category with specific operating conditions. A privately built aircraft is not automatically a class-labelled C0 product. Treat 250 g as a valuable design target; measure the complete take-off mass and verify the exact operational category, registration, training and airspace requirements before flight. GCAA UAS portal ↗

What you should understand now

Does “four-inch” describe the whole frame width?
No. In FPV use it normally describes nominal propeller diameter. Wheelbase is a separate motor-to-motor measurement.
Why use replaceable arms?
They isolate likely crash damage so one arm can be replaced instead of discarding the complete frame.
Can we claim this prototype is under 250 g?
No. The complete take-off mass must be measured, and legal class/operation conditions require a separate check.

Chapter 3 · Propulsion

Choose a system, not isolated parts.

A propeller loads a motor. The motor loads an electronic speed controller (ESC) and battery. Change one link and every later link needs checking.

The compatibility chain
01Mission + mass
→
02Propeller
→
03Motor size + KV
→
04Battery voltage
→
05ESC current
→
06Battery capacity

The motor

It converts switched electrical power into rotation.

1404 usually means an approximately 14 mm stator diameter and 4 mm stator height—not the motor's outside size. KV is an approximate no-load speed constant in revolutions per minute per volt. Higher KV is not “more powerful”; with the same voltage it tries to turn faster and may overload the motor on too large a propeller.

  • Connects toThree ESC phase wires; propeller and frame mount.
  • Must matchProp size/load, battery voltage, mounting holes, shaft and prop hub.
  • Wrong choiceOverheating, excessive current, poor thrust or a propeller that cannot mount.
Make or buy?

Buy motors in year one. Own test data, accepted alternates, mounting interface and supplier change control. Motor production needs magnetic materials, winding, balancing, bearings and specialised quality equipment.

The propeller

It is a rotating wing that accelerates air downward.

Diameter controls the swept disc; pitch describes how aggressively the blade is shaped to advance through air; blade count changes load and response. The set needs the correct clockwise and counter-clockwise shapes and the exact hub mounting for the motors.

  • Connects toMotor shaft/hub and the surrounding air.
  • Must matchMotor, voltage, clearance, rotation and mounting.
  • Wrong choiceCollision, reversed thrust, vibration, loose mounting or overload.
Make or buy?

Buy propellers. Injection moulding and aerodynamic balance make small-volume in-house production unrealistic. We own clearance rules, acceptance checks and alternate qualification.

Why the chain runs in this order

  1. Mission and estimated mass tell us how much thrust and endurance are needed.
  2. Propeller is chosen to move the required air within safe size and noise limits.
  3. Motor size and KV must turn that propeller efficiently at the chosen voltage.
  4. Battery voltage affects speed and current for that motor/prop combination.
  5. ESC current capacity needs real margin above measured or credible test current, at realistic cooling.
  6. Battery capacity/current capability must support the total current and desired usable energy without excessive mass or voltage sag.

Three worked architecture examples

PlatformPlanning chainEvidenceStill unknown
4-inch candidateCompact learning mission → 4″ prop → EX1404 2750KV → 4S → 40 A all-in-one FC/ESC → 850mAh candidateManufacturer motor bench dataRetail fit auditComplete mass, static thrust/current, temperatures, sag, endurance
5-inch exampleMore room/energy → 5″ prop → common 22xx-class motor → 4S/6S choice → matching ESC → capacity by measured missionTeaching architecture onlyEvery exact part, cost and measurement
X500-style referencePayload/development → larger prop → lower-KV larger motor → higher-energy pack → separate ESCs → capacity by payload/enduranceHolybro reference specsOriginal product mission and complete configuration
Go deeper · thrust-to-weight

Total measured maximum thrust divided by measured take-off weight is the thrust-to-weight ratio. A value above 1 means it can rise; usable control margin needs more than bare equality. Do not select a target ratio without defining mission, safety and handling requirements. Manufacturer bench tests are useful screening evidence, not an assembled-aircraft result.

Dated retail snapshotsFour-motor pack: USD 38.99 · propeller set: USD 3.69 · exact variants must be rechecked.

What you should understand now

Why must propeller, motor, battery and ESC be selected together?
The prop determines aerodynamic load; motor and voltage determine how it is driven; this creates current that the ESC and battery must safely supply.
Does higher motor KV mean more power?
No. KV mainly relates no-load speed per volt. Real power and suitability depend on motor construction, voltage, propeller load, current and cooling.

Chapter 4 · Electricity

Pressure, flow, power, stored energy.

Electricity becomes easier when four ideas stay separate: voltage pushes, current flows, power is the rate of work, and energy is how much work the battery can provide over time.

V
Voltage

Electrical “pressure” between two points. Cells in series add voltage.

A
Current

Rate of electrical charge flow, measured in amperes.

W
Power

Rate of energy use. Power = voltage × current.

Wh
Energy

Stored work capacity. Watt-hours = nominal volts × amp-hours.

A conventional lithium-polymer (LiPo) cell is commonly treated as about 3.7 V nominal. 4S means four cells in series, about 14.8 V nominal. The voltage changes while charging and under load. 850 mAh means 0.85 amp-hours of charge; it does not directly state flight time.

Battery energy calculator

First understand the inputs: cell count sets nominal voltage; capacity describes charge. Their product estimates stored energy for comparing packs. It does not predict usable flight time.

Nominal voltage14.8 V
Nominal energy12.58 Wh
Ideal time, not real flight5.1 min

Real usable time is lower and must be measured with a safe reserve because voltage sag, efficiency, manoeuvres, temperature and battery condition matter.

What can go wrong

Polarity and short circuit

Connect positive to negative incorrectly and components can fail instantly. A short circuit creates a very low-resistance path and enormous current. Inspect, test continuity and use current-limited first power.

C-rating

A label claiming a discharge multiplier. It can screen candidates, but production qualification needs measured voltage sag and temperature under the real load.

Voltage sag

Internal resistance makes battery voltage fall when current rises. Excessive sag reduces available thrust and produces heat even when the resting voltage looked acceptable.

Connectors

Type, current capability, physical size and polarity must match the aircraft, charger and service process. A hidden adapter is still a required part and failure point.

Charging is a controlled process

The charger returns energy while monitoring the battery; it cannot make a damaged pack safe.

  • BeforeInspect pack, connector and balance lead; confirm settings.
  • DuringAttend charging on a noncombustible location with an emergency plan.
  • AfterVerify cell balance, temperature and storage plan.
Lithium battery fire riskDamage, overheating, overcharge or short circuit can trigger thermal runaway. Do not charge a swollen or damaged pack or improvise chemistry/cell-count settings. Follow current transport rules and create a site-specific emergency plan. FAA lithium battery overview ↗
Make or buy?

Buy certified cells/packs and chargers. Year-one knowledge we own: connector/polarity specification, incoming inspection, storage/charge procedure, pack traceability, retirement criteria and measured sag/temperature.

Go deeper · nominal voltage versus real voltage

Nominal voltage is a comparison label, not a fixed reading. Cell voltage rises during charging and falls under load. A production test must define where voltage is measured, the load, temperature, battery state and acceptable reserve. Open-circuit voltage alone cannot prove current capability.

Dated retail snapshotsBattery USD 14.99 · charger USD 29.99 · safety bag USD 9.99. Recheck exact variants and availability before purchase.

What you should understand now

Where does battery power travel?
From battery and main connector into the ESC/power distribution, then as switched three-phase power to each motor. Regulators also provide lower voltages to electronics.
Why is mAh not flight time?
It describes charge capacity. Flight time also depends on current demand, voltage, efficiency, reserve, temperature, battery condition and manoeuvres.

Chapter 5 · Control electronics

One decides. One switches power.

The flight controller is the decision-making computer. The electronic speed controller, or ESC, is the fast power switch that actually drives each motor.

Flight controller (FC)
Reads pilot commands and motion sensors, calculates corrections and requests motor speeds.
Electronic speed controller (ESC)
Rapidly switches battery power through the three motor wires to create the requested rotation.

Sensors tell the computer what happened

A gyroscope measures rotational movement. An accelerometer measures specific force and helps estimate which way is down when conditions permit. They do not “know” the mission. Firmware combines their measurements with pilot input and configuration.

Power flow and information flow are different

Power · high current and regulated rails
Batterymain voltage
→
ESC power stagehigh-current switching
→
Motorsthree phases each
+
5 V regulatorreceiver/camera/VTX if rated
Information · requests and measurements
Receiverpilot request
→
FC + gyrocompute correction
→
ESC commanddigital language such as DShot
→
Motor responseaircraft moves
↺

How to read a wiring map

A pad label states an electrical job, not merely where a coloured wire goes.

  • BAT / GNDBattery positive and common return; polarity is critical.
  • 5VRegulated power rail with a finite current capacity.
  • TX / RXTransmit and receive serial data; normally cross TX to RX.
  • CAM / VTXAnalog video in/out where onboard display is inserted.
  • M1–M4Motor outputs that must match physical motor order.

Firmware fits a job

Betaflight

Best fit for Prototype 1's manually piloted FPV learning: direct setup, responsive multirotor control and common small-board support.

ArduPilot

Better when the mission needs richer autonomy, navigation, mission planning, broad sensor integration and vehicle types.

PX4

Strong development/autonomy platform with modular architecture and research/industrial ecosystem. Appropriate for a later X500-style path.

Official documentationBetaflight · ArduPilot · PX4

Make or buy?

Buy the electronics. Own wiring architecture, firmware version and configuration, provisioning process, calibration, acceptance tests, backups, revision records and alternate qualification. Later custom electronics require a larger design/compliance/supply programme.

Go deeper · power rails and noise

The battery rail carries large switching currents. Regulators create lower-voltage rails for logic and peripherals. Motor switching can inject electrical noise; layout, grounding, capacitor choice, wire routing and tested peripheral loads matter. “5 V” identifies voltage, not unlimited current.

Dated retail snapshotCandidate all-in-one FC/ESC: USD 79.99 · not a production quotation.

What you should understand now

What is the difference between the flight controller and ESC?
The flight controller decides what each motor should do using pilot commands and sensors. The ESC switches battery power to make each motor do it.
What is DShot?
One digital language a flight controller can use to send requested motor commands to compatible ESC firmware. It is not the motor power itself.

Chapter 6 · Radio links

The pilot sends intent. The camera sends sight.

Control and first-person-view video use separate hardware and can fail separately. Understanding both paths is essential to design safe lost-link behaviour.

ExpressLRS control link

ExpressLRS is an open radio-control system connecting a compatible transmitter and receiver.

  • PathHands → handheld radio → radio waves → aircraft receiver → flight controller.
  • Must matchFrequency band, firmware family, binding phrase/settings, serial protocol and failsafe plan.
  • Wrong choiceNo bind, unstable link, illegal operation or unsafe lost-control behaviour.

Official ExpressLRS firmware guidance ↗

Video is a second chain

Why a laptop cannot directly receive it

An ordinary laptop has no tuner/demodulator for analog 5.8 GHz FPV radio.

The video is not Wi-Fi and is not arriving as a USB camera stream. A laptop would need a separate compatible radio receiver and usually a video-capture device, adding complexity and latency. A direct analog receiver monitor is simpler for first learning.

Analog versus digital video

Analog

Lower-cost equipment, visible degradation as signal weakens and simple direct receivers. Lower image quality; channel/power legality still matters.

Digital

Encodes/compresses the picture and needs a matching digital ecosystem. Usually clearer video and higher cost; latency and failure behaviour depend on the system.

Lost control is not lost video.If control is lost, preconfigured failsafe behaviour must put the aircraft into the safest achievable state for the verified platform and operation. If video is lost but control remains, the pilot needs a rehearsed legal/safe response using visual line of sight or an allowed observer. Do not invent an automatic “return home” on a P1 that has no verified navigation system.
Georgia radio boundaryThe national frequency plan does not by itself authorise every channel, modulation, antenna or power level. Obtain written Georgian Communications Commission interpretation for the exact 2.4 GHz control and airborne 5.8 GHz video devices/settings before flight or product definition. Aircraft operation also remains subject to GCAA rules.
Make or buy?

Buy radio, camera and video electronics. Own antenna location, harnessing, configuration, failsafe test, RF documentation, traceability and supplier evidence. Future custom RF hardware adds certification and compliance work.

Go deeper · antennas and link margin

An antenna converts electrical radio-frequency energy to electromagnetic waves and back. Orientation, nearby conductive carbon, damaged coax, connector loss, transmit power, receiver sensitivity, interference and terrain all affect a link. A high power label or desktop range test is not a safe-range guarantee.

Dated retail snapshotsRadio USD 71.49 · cells USD 14.99 · receiver USD 15.99 · camera USD 9.99 · VTX USD 22.99 · monitor USD 84.99. These are learning-system references, not RF approval or volume quotes.

What you should understand now

Where do pilot commands travel?
Radio sticks → transmitter → radio signal → aircraft receiver → flight controller → ESC commands → motor response.
Where does video travel?
Camera → video transmitter and antenna → radio path → matching video receiver → screen.
Why can’t a normal laptop receive analog FPV directly?
It lacks the specialised analog 5.8 GHz radio receiver and demodulator. Extra receiver/capture hardware would be required.

Chapter 7 · Build sequence

Build in an order that makes mistakes cheap to find.

The aim is not merely to power the drone. Each stage creates evidence and has a stop condition before more energy, complexity or propeller risk is introduced.

  1. Verify exact parts

    Record item, variant, revision, quantity and visible condition. Similar names are not interchangeable.

    Stop if any exact variant or manual is unresolved.

  2. Dry-fit the complete aircraft

    Assemble without final wiring. Confirm mounting patterns, stack height, camera, antenna, connector and battery space.

    Stop if a part needs unsafe force, drilling or hidden adapters.

  3. Check propeller clearance

    Use exact unpowered props and include wires, battery and straps. Remove props again immediately.

    Stop if any swept disc or flex margin intersects hardware.

  4. Plan wiring and practise soldering

    Draw the power/signal map. Prove joints on coupons before touching the flight controller.

    Stop if joints are dull, bridged, weak or uninspected.

  5. Install power lead and capacitor

    Use correct polarity, wire size, insulation and strain relief. Keep conductive debris away.

    Stop before battery power; inspect under magnification.

  6. Continuity and polarity checks

    Use the multimeter to confirm no short between main rails and correct connector polarity.

    Any unexpected continuity means no power.

  7. Current-limited first power

    Use a smoke stopper/current limiter, observe, smell and touch only after power is removed.

    Trip, heat, smoke or wrong voltage: disconnect and diagnose.

  8. Add one subsystem at a time

    Receiver, camera and VTX are installed and tested as separate changes.

    A new fault belongs to the latest controlled change.

  9. Back up firmware configuration

    Record board target, firmware, settings, wiring, receiver/VTX configuration and serial number.

    No uncontrolled update or copied internet configuration.

  10. Test motors without propellers

    Verify motor order and requested direction at low power with a restrained aircraft.

    Props remain removed until all configuration/failsafe checks pass.

  11. Controlled first hover

    Only after legal site, weather, pilot/observer, emergency plan and preflight gate are satisfied.

    Unexpected sound, vibration, control or temperature ends the test.

  12. Post-flight inspection

    Disconnect, inspect fasteners, arms, props, wiring, battery and temperatures; record findings before the next flight.

Propellers off means physically removed.Remove them for firmware work, receiver and failsafe configuration, and initial motor testing. Software disarm is not a physical barrier. Betaflight setup guidance ↗
Manufacturing lens

Assembly is a real manufacturing process. Create a controlled traveller/checklist, calibrated tools where needed, solder acceptance samples, torque/fastener rules, configuration backups, serial identity, failure log and final acceptance record.

Dated retail snapshotsTool kit USD 100.49 · smoke stopper USD 18.99 · strap pair USD 4.99. Local personal protective equipment (PPE) and consumables remain additional planning allowances.

What you should understand now

Why dry-fit before soldering?
It finds mechanical incompatibility while parts and wire lengths can still change cheaply, before permanent joints or power create risk.
What must happen before first battery power?
Exact parts/manuals verified, wiring inspected, polarity and continuity checked, propellers removed, area controlled and a current limiter ready.

Chapter 8 · Frame engineering

A frame begins as requirements, not a shape.

The geometry must carry known loads, place every subsystem, permit assembly and inspection, and fail in repairable ways. A beautiful CAD model without controlled requirements is not yet an engineering design.

From need to controlled design

Customer / learning needwhat job and environment?
Engineering requirementsinterfaces and measurable limits
Concept + CADgeometry and materials
Prototype + testsproduce evidence
Failure → revisioncontrolled drawing released

Follow the load

↟
Motor thrust

Motor mount → arm → centre plates → opposite arms/body.

⌁
Motor torque

Twists arms and joints; repeated cycles can loosen fasteners.

↓
Landing/crash

Impact enters feet, arms or camera protection and travels to the centre.

≋
Vibration

Propeller/motor imbalance reaches sensors, solder joints and camera.

Material is a system choice

Computer numerical control (CNC) means a machine follows programmed tool motion to cut a controlled shape.

MaterialUseful propertyWeakness / riskLikely use
Carbon-fibre laminate plateHigh stiffness for mass; flat CNC geometryDirectional laminate, edge damage, hazardous conductive dustOutsourced arms and centre plates
Carbon tubeEfficient long memberJoint design, drilling and crush riskLarger X500-style arms/landing gear
AluminiumMachinable, inspectable, locally availableHeavier for equal bending stiffness; can permanently bendBrackets, prototypes, fixtures
Engineering nylon / glass-filled nylonTough complex shapes; moulding/printing pathsMoisture, anisotropy, creep and process controlConnectors, mounts, guards
Thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU)Flexible and impact-tolerantToo soft for primary precision structureSacrificial bumpers, antenna/camera protection

Geometry rules a beginner can see

Replaceable armsLocalise likely damage and reduce service cost.
Sacrificial partsCheap guards fail before cameras or plates.
Generous filletsRounded internal corners reduce stress concentration.
Hole edge distanceMaterial around a hole carries fastener load.
Laminate directionCarbon strength/stiffness depend on internal fibre directions, not surface appearance.
Fastener accessA design must allow the real tool to assemble and repair it.

Files and control

CAD and exchange

CAD is the editable design model. DXF commonly carries 2D cut profiles. STEP carries neutral 3D geometry. STL is a triangle mesh commonly used for printing; it is poor as the master manufacturing definition.

Drawing and revision

A controlled drawing identifies part number, revision, material, thickness, critical dimensions, tolerances, datums, finish and inspection notes. A datum is an agreed measurement reference. A tolerance is allowed variation—not permission for an arbitrary shape.

Design for the whole lifecycle

Design for manufacture (DFM) asks whether the chosen process can make the geometry repeatably and economically.

DFMavailable material, cutters, setups, radii
→
ASSEMBLYfew fasteners, tool access, no reversal
→
INSPECTIONcritical dimensions reachable by gauges
→
REPAIRcommon damage replaceable
→
PACKAGINGedges, loose hardware and identity controlled
Go deeper · stress concentrations and thickness

Sharp internal corners, closely spaced holes and abrupt width changes concentrate stress. Increasing plate thickness often increases bending stiffness strongly, but adds mass and does not cure a bad load path. Numeric thickness and acceptance limits must come from requirements, analysis, coupons, arm tests and flight evidence—not copying one hobby frame.

What we can own in year one

Mission/requirements, interface control, CAD, drawings, revisions, material specification, inspection plan, test method, supplier feedback and failure analysis. Outsourced cutting does not surrender design ownership.

What you should understand now

What does the frame need to survive?
Motor thrust and torque, landing and crash loads, vibration, fastener loads, battery/payload inertia, environment and repeated fatigue—all defined by the intended mission and repair plan.
Which frame parts could we manufacture?
Original plate/tube structure, printed nylon/TPU mounts, fixtures, harnesses and final assembly. Carbon cutting should initially be outsourced while we own its specification and inspection.

Chapter 9 · Manufacturing process

The machine is one small part of a safe process.

Cutting carbon is not “buy a router and press start.” The complete cell includes containment, extraction, workholding, cutters, measurement, cleaning, waste control, maintenance and trained people.

Separate workspacenot living or electronics assembly space
Closed enclosurecontains chips and fine dust
Source extractioncapture near the cutter
Suitable filtrationdesigned for the hazard
Workholding + toolsrepeatable cutting without release
Metrologygauges, calipers, fixtures
PPE + cleanupdocumented exposure controls
Waste + maintenancesafe disposal and sustained performance

Compare the processes

ProcessBest useMain limitationYear-one position
Outsourced CNC carbon cuttingControlled flat plates, holes and slotsSupplier lead time, communication and minimum chargesRecommended first
In-house CNC routingFast iterations and repeatable profilesDust hazard, tool wear, fixturing, maintenance and capitalOnly after gates
Manual cutting/drillingRough experiments or repair fixturesExposure, poor repeatability and edge qualityNot production route
WaterjetCold cutting at capable service bureauAbrasive/water effects, fixturing and edge/delamination validationSupplier process to qualify
LaserUseful for some polymers/metalsCarbon composite resin/fibre heat damage, fumes and poor edge qualityAvoid for carbon laminate unless specialised proven process
3D printingMounts, ducts, guards, jigs and fit modelsAnisotropy, moisture, creep, finish and material/process variabilityBring in early
Moulded compositesCurved shells and integrated formsTooling, layup, cure and repeatability complexityLater product-specific path
Injection mouldingHigh-volume repeatable polymer partsExpensive tooling and design freeze riskOnly after demand/design stabilise
Carbon dust is an exposure and contamination hazard.Machining can release fine, abrasive and electrically conductive dust that irritates and can short electronics. Do not cut carbon in living space or beside electronics assembly. A dust boot alone is not a complete control system. Use professional site/process design, enclosure, source capture, suitable filtration, personal protective equipment, controlled cleanup and waste handling. Supplier safety data ↗

Why outsourced carbon is the intelligent first factory

You still manufacture knowledge

You control requirements, part revision, CAD/drawing, material/layup specification, supplier approval, first article, inspection, assembly, tests and non-conformance. The supplier performs one hazardous conversion step.

You avoid buying uncertainty

Before geometry, volume and demand stabilise, an internal cell may sit idle or lock the product to the wrong process. Two suppliers can produce comparable samples while you learn which specifications matter.

Do not buy a carbon router until

  • An original frame revision has passed defined mechanical and controlled flight tests.
  • At least two external suppliers have quoted the controlled drawing and material.
  • Expected annual demand and external lead-time cost are recorded.
  • A separate workspace, extraction, filtration, fire/occupational and waste plan is approved.
  • Payback includes labour, scrap, tooling, maintenance, filters, downtime, metrology and realistic utilisation.
Go deeper · machine utilisation and payback

A machine rate must include depreciation or financing, operator/setup time, cutters, extraction filters, energy, calibration, maintenance, scrap, floor space and downtime divided by realistic productive hours—not 24 hours per day. Internal cost only beats outsourcing when volume, lead time or confidentiality benefits survive this complete comparison.

Jigs turn skill into repeatability

Assembly nestLocates plates and arms from datums while tightening.
Hole fixtureControls repeated tube/plate holes without hand measuring.
Go/no-go gaugeQuickly checks a motor pattern, arm width or stack interface.
Harness boardDefines wire lengths, branches and connector orientation.
Bend-test fixtureApplies repeatable support span, load and measurement.
Balance fixtureChecks battery/payload centre-of-gravity range.

What you should understand now

Why should carbon cutting initially be outsourced?
It lets us learn and control the product—design, specification, quality and tests—without prematurely buying a hazardous, capital-intensive process before volume and geometry are proven.
Is a CNC router the complete workstation?
No. It also needs dedicated space, enclosure, source extraction, suitable filtration, workholding, cutters, metrology, PPE, cleanup, waste handling, inspection and maintenance.

Chapter 10 · Evidence

Quality means proving the released revision was built.

Inspection finds whether a requirement was met. Testing finds whether the design or process can survive its intended job. Both need records tied to a part, revision, lot and serial number.

Quality flow

Incomingright material, quantity, condition, certificates
First articlecomplete check of first new revision/process
In processcatch error before it is hidden
Finalcomplete product and configuration
Traceabilityserial, lot, result, disposition

Four levels of inspection

01
Incoming

Identity, revision, material, damage, key dimensions and supplier documents.

02
First article

First part from a new design/revision/process checked against all requirements before batch release.

03
In process

Checks performed while correction is still possible: harness, torque, orientation, solder joints.

04
Final

As-built configuration, functional test, appearance, packaging and record completeness.

What happens when a part fails

Non-conformancerequirement not met
→
Quarantineprevent accidental use
→
Dispositionrework, use-as-is with authority, return or scrap
→
Root causewhen risk/repetition warrants
→
Corrective actionprove recurrence reduced

Rework follows an approved instruction and is re-inspected. Scrap is made unusable or controlled so it cannot re-enter production. “It looks fine” is not an authorised disposition.

Tests build from cheap evidence to flight

TestWhat it teachesRecord
Material couponSupplier/layup/process comparison at small scaleLot, geometry, fixture, load/deflection/failure
Arm bendingStiffness, permanent set and failure modeSpan, load point, direction, revision, curve/photos
Fastener retentionJoint loosening, crushing or pull-outFastener, torque method, cycles and post-check
VibrationSensor noise, resonance, loose hardware and image qualityProp/motor state, firmware logs, mounting and spectrum/observations
TemperatureMotor, ESC, regulator, battery and printed-part marginAmbient, load profile, location, time and maximum
FatigueRepeated-load degradation rather than one overloadCycle shape/count, inspection interval and failure
Crash/repairDamage localisation, service time and hidden damageControlled case, parts, time, cost and post-repair acceptance
Flight acceptanceComplete system under controlled operationConfiguration, pilot/site, checklist, logs and post-flight inspection
Numeric pass limits are deliberately open.We do not yet have original-frame load, vibration, thermal or fatigue requirements. Define them from the intended civilian mission, hazards and design evidence; then freeze the test method before comparing revisions. Do not invent impressive numbers.

The minimum traceability record

IdentityPart/product number, revision and serial number.
MaterialsSupplier, lot, certificate and received condition.
ProcessOperator, date, equipment, fixture and controlled instruction.
ConfigurationHardware variants, firmware and settings backup.
ResultsMeasurements, test data, failures and acceptance.
DispositionRework, deviation, return or scrap authorisation.

What you should understand now

What is the difference between inspection and testing?
Inspection checks conformity to specified requirements; testing applies defined conditions to learn or prove performance. A dimensional check cannot prove crash survival, and a successful flight cannot prove every drawing dimension.
Why record serial numbers?
To connect each aircraft/part to its revision, lots, build process, configuration, test results, failures and any later corrective action.

Chapter 11 · Economics

A parts list is not a product cost.

A conforming product consumes material, purchased components, labour, machine time, inspection, packaging, logistics, warranty, support and cash while inventory is waiting.

Verified retail snapshotObserved exact listing, dated

Not a volume quote, landed cost or stock assurance.

Planning allowanceBudget placeholder

Useful for avoiding hidden cost; replace before commitment.

RFQ / unknownEvidence not yet obtained

Never silently convert an unknown into a fact.

Measured resultProduced by our controlled test

State method, unit, configuration and date.

The complete cost stack

Parts + materialpurchased inputs
+
Labour + machineconversion
+
Scrap + inspectionyield and proof
=
Factory costconforming unit
+
Freight + tax + packinbound/landed
=
Landed costready to sell
+

Working capital is cash tied up between paying suppliers and receiving customer payment. A unit can look profitable and still exhaust cash if minimum orders and lead times are large. One-time engineering and capital equipment must be financed or amortised; they do not disappear.

Transparent frame cost calculator

Every input below is initially a teaching assumption in USD. “Good units” means units that pass; scrap makes each good unit carry part of failed attempts.

Factory cost$63.56
Landed + support + engineering$110.09
Illustrative selling price$169.37

This models a frame, not the complete aircraft. It excludes channel fees and company overhead unless you add them into an input. Replace inputs with supplier quotes, time studies and measured yield.

Scale changes the question

QuantityMain questionEvidence requiredTypical trap
1Can one coherent aircraft be built, tested and repaired?As-built record and measurementsCalling one success production-ready
10Can the same revision be repeated?Build time, first-pass yield, fixture feedback, traceabilityExpert hand-fitting hidden as labour
100Can suppliers/inventory/training sustain a pilot batch?Quotes, yields, warranty and cash modelIgnoring rework, packaging and working capital
1,000Which suppliers/processes need capacity or automation?Capacity, process capability, PCN/EOL and alternatesRetail stock presented as supply assurance
5,000Does tooling/internalisation reduce total cost?Validated demand, amortisation and field failure dataBuying tooling before design stabilises
RFQ gate before production BOM freezeRequest identical controlled packages at 100, 1,000 and 5,000 units. Ask for price, minimum order quantity, samples/tooling, lead time, monthly capacity, exact material/process/site, inspection/traceability, product-change notification (PCN), end-of-life (EOL) notice, alternates, Incoterm, payment and quote validity.
Go deeper · gross margin is not profit

Gross margin compares selling price with the cost basis assigned to the unit. Company operating expenses, product development, sales, administration, financing and tax can remain outside it. The calculator is a sensitivity tool; a viable business needs a cash-flow model and verified demand as well.

What you should understand now

What costs exist beyond the parts list?
Labour, machine time, scrap/rework, inspection, packaging, freight, tax/customs, warranty, support, overhead, engineering, equipment, channel cost and working capital.
Why does scale require new evidence?
Repeatability, supplier capacity, inventory cash, process capability, lifecycle terms and field failures do not appear in a single prototype or retail listing.

Chapter 12 · Decision

Four-inch wins the learning experiment—for now.

Keep the compact analog-FPV quad as the provisional Prototype 1 architecture because it teaches the complete system at the lowest currently audited aircraft checkout. Run original-frame development in parallel and outsource carbon cutting first.

This is not a purchase order, final product or production BOM. The decision must be revisited after learning gates and a fresh audit.

Provisional recommendation

4-inch analog FPV

Best current balance of beginner cost, complete system learning, repair and frame-manufacturing relevance.

5-inch analog FPV

Switch only with better controlled supply/fit evidence, accepted higher energy and safe test space.

X500-style platform

Switch when the goal becomes payload, navigation/autonomy or modular customer validation—and the much higher cost is accepted.

One understandable comparison

Criterion4-inch analog FPV5-inch analog FPVX500-style

Frame manufacturingFlat plates/arms + printed pod; useful first processSimilar flat-plate process with more roomPlates, tubes, connectors, rails and more fixtures
RepairabilityReplaceable arms; compact accessOften easier access and replaceable armsModular but more parts/calibration

Path to Georgian productFastest low-cost skills and original frame workPotential rugged FPV/frame path if demand existsBest later inspection/research reference if customers need it

What must be measured before freezing P1

  • Mass + balanceComplete take-off mass and centre of gravity with exact battery, straps and props.
  • MechanicalProp clearance, arm/fastener behaviour, crash damage and repair time.
  • PropulsionExact-prop static thrust/current, motor and ESC temperature.
  • EnergyBattery sag, representative current, usable endurance with reserve.
  • ControlVibration logs, motor order/direction, failsafe and handling.
  • LinksControl/video behaviour and written Georgian RF interpretation.
  • OperationGCAA category, registration/training/airspace and safe test facility.
  • Supply100/1,000/5,000 quotes, alternates, capacity, revision, PCN and EOL terms.

A realistic first year

Months 1–2

Complete fundamentals, simulator practice, solder coupons, CAD fit models and props-off configuration learning. Do not purchase flight hardware until the explicit pre-purchase gate.

Months 3–4

Refresh exact BOM, regulation, shipping and safe facility. If authorised, build and commission one controlled retail-component prototype.

Months 5–7

Write original frame requirements, obtain two outsourced carbon samples, inspect/test, revise and only then run controlled flight tests.

Months 8–10

Build five same-revision engineering units; track yield, build time, rework and serial records. Conduct legal civilian customer/problem discovery without claiming demand.

Months 11–12

Run a ten-unit engineering batch if evidence supports it. Complete cost/working-capital/warranty model and decide whether to continue, revise or stop. Re-evaluate in-house carbon only against full process economics.

Year-one internal scopeOriginal requirements and CAD, drawings/revisions, printed mounts and fixtures, harnesses, assembly, firmware provisioning, inspection, testing, traceability and packaging. Purchase motors, electronics, sensors, radio parts, camera, batteries, propellers, raw carbon and standard hardware initially.

Primary evidence and boundaries

Evidence was checked 11 August 2026 unless a dated snapshot is shown. Live price, stock, regulation, exact RF classification and product revision must be refreshed before purchase, flight or production commitment.

Known gapsNo Georgian customer-demand evidence, no written ComCom interpretation for these exact devices, no measured assembled aircraft, no controlled five-inch BOM, no original-frame numeric requirements, and no 100/1,000/5,000-unit quotations. These are next tasks, not facts to invent.

Final beginner comprehension test

If any answer is unclear, use the chapter link in the answer and revisit it.

1. Why four motors?
They create lift and independent control around roll, pitch and yaw with a simple layout. Revisit Chapter 1.
2. FC versus ESC?
The flight controller decides; the ESC switches motor power. Chapter 5.
3. Why select prop, motor, battery and ESC together?
They form one load/current/voltage chain. Chapter 3.
4–6. Where do power, command and video travel?
Power: battery → ESC → motors. Command: radio → receiver → FC → ESC. Video: camera → VTX → receiver monitor. Chapters 0, 5 and 6.
7. Why not a laptop for direct analog FPV?
It lacks a compatible 5.8 GHz analog receiver/demodulator. Chapter 6.
8–10. Frame loads, manufacturable parts and outsourcing?
The frame carries motor, impact, vibration and payload/battery loads. We can own/design frame, mounts, fixtures, harnesses and assembly. Carbon is outsourced first because the process is hazardous and volume/process economics are unproven. Chapters 8–9.
11. Costs beyond parts?
Labour, machine, scrap, inspection, packaging, logistics, tax, warranty, support, engineering, equipment and working capital. Chapter 11.
12. What before P1 freeze?
Measured mass, balance, clearances, thrust/current, temperatures, sag/endurance, vibration, failures/repair, legal/RF conditions, safe site and production-scale supplier evidence. This chapter.

Persistent reference

Plain-language glossary
Aircraft / drone / UAS
The flying vehicle; an unmanned aircraft system (UAS) also includes equipment and people needed to operate it.
FPV
First-person view: live onboard video used by the pilot.
FC
Flight controller: computer that reads motion and commands motor changes.
ESC
Electronic speed controller: fast power switch that drives a motor.
VTX / receiver / transmitter
Video transmitter; device that receives a radio signal; device that sends one.
LiPo / S / mAh / Wh
Lithium-polymer battery; series-cell count; milliamp-hours of charge; watt-hours of energy.
KV
Approximate motor no-load speed constant in revolutions per minute per volt.
Centre of gravity (CoG)
The balance point of the complete aircraft including battery and payload.
CAD / DXF / STEP / STL
Editable computer-aided design; 2D profile exchange; neutral 3D exchange; triangle mesh often used for printing.
Datum / tolerance
An agreed measurement reference; permitted variation from a nominal value.
BOM / revision
Bill of materials; controlled version of a product, part or document.
RFQ / MOQ
Request for quotation; minimum order quantity.
PCN / EOL
Product change notification; end of life.
First article
First unit from a new design, revision, supplier or process inspected fully before batch release.
Traceability
Ability to connect a unit to its parts/lots, revision, process, configuration, tests and disposition.
Factory / landed / selling cost
Cost to produce; cost after inbound logistics/duties; customer price after commercial costs and margin.
Working capital
Cash tied up while paying suppliers, holding inventory and waiting for customers to pay.
